theory.title: Inequality and Social Mobility: language and critical analysis
theory.explanation: Develop C1-level communication for structural inequality, opportunity and social mobility. This mission examines the concepts, evidence and competing interpretations relevant to the topic. Learners practise precise terminology, nuanced qualification and coherent argument while distinguishing established information from inference.
theory.tip: Define the issue, identify the evidence behind each claim and qualify conclusions where context or uncertainty limits what can be established.

reading.english:
Social inequality is reproduced through interacting mechanisms rather than a single cause. Differences in wealth can affect access to education, housing and professional networks; these advantages may then accumulate across generations. Formal equality of opportunity does not guarantee that people begin from comparable positions.

Social mobility describes movement between socioeconomic positions, but aggregate mobility figures can conceal unequal experiences across regions and groups. A policy may improve average outcomes while leaving entrenched barriers largely untouched.

Careful analysis distinguishes individual choices from structural constraints. This does not deny personal agency; it recognises that choices are made within conditions that distribute risks and opportunities unevenly.

listening.english:
Bringing Personal Narratives Together

Understanding identity requires more than one explanatory lens. Memory shapes the stories people tell about themselves, but recollection is selective and can be influenced by later information. Motivation helps explain choices, although neither personality traits nor external incentives provide a complete account of behaviour. A balanced interpretation considers context as well as individual agency.

Relationships also shape self-understanding. Trust, reciprocity and boundaries influence how people participate in social roles, while emotional literacy can help them respond to tension without treating an immediate reaction as definitive. During life transitions, resilience may involve revising assumptions, seeking support and adapting routines rather than simply returning to a previous state.

An integrated perspective does not flatten these differences into a single formula. It asks how memory, motivation, relationships, emotion and social context interact in a particular case. Strong communication reflects that complexity: claims are qualified, evidence is weighed and conclusions remain open to revision when new information emerges.

Conclusions require qualification when uncertainty remains, and a balanced judgement should reflect the strength of the evidence. The final conclusion should remain proportionate.
